## Preventive Medicine
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/preventive-medicine

Prevention is the most powerful medicine. From core vaccines to parasite protection — keeping your pet healthy before illness strikes.

Q: What age should I start vaccinating my puppy?
A: Puppies should start their first vaccination at 6–8 weeks of age. The core series runs until 16 weeks, with a booster at 1 year. We'll give you a complete schedule at your first visit.

Q: How often does my adult dog need vaccines?
A: In India, annual vaccination is recommended for most pets. Vaccination schedules may vary based on age, lifestyle, travel, boarding requirements and health status. Dr. Pritesh will advise a personalised plan during your visit.

Q: My cat stays indoors — does it still need vaccines?
A: Yes. Indoor cats can still be exposed to infectious diseases through visitors, other pets, and contaminated objects brought into the home. Annual vaccination remains important.

Q: What tick prevention product do you recommend for Pune?
A: Parasite prevention recommendations are based on your pet's age, lifestyle, and medical history. Our veterinarians will advise the most suitable option during your consultation.

Q: Can I deworm my pet at home without a vet?
A: Over-the-counter dewormers only cover some worm types. A stool test tells us exactly what parasite is present so we can treat it accurately. We recommend a proper parasite screening at least once a year.

## Clinical Medicine
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/clinical-medicine

A thorough, unhurried examination is the foundation of good medicine. Dr. Pritesh takes the time to examine every system, understand the history, and explain the findings clearly.

Q: What does a consultation cost at Shivraj Pet Clinic & Lab?
A: Consultation fee is ₹300, payable at the clinic. All costs for diagnostics or treatment are discussed and agreed upfront — no surprise bills.

Q: Can I come without an appointment?
A: Walk-ins are accepted during clinic hours. For complex cases or if you want to ensure a specific time slot, calling ahead is recommended. Emergencies are always seen immediately.

Q: Do you treat cats and exotic animals, not just dogs?
A: Yes — Dr. Pritesh treats dogs, cats, birds, rabbits, turtles, guinea pigs, hamsters, and other exotic species. We're one of the few clinics in PCMC with this range of expertise.

Q: What if my pet needs multiple tests the same day?
A: We prefer to complete diagnostics in one visit where possible. Our in-house lab, X-ray, and ultrasound mean most diagnostic workups can be done same-day without referral.

Q: Can I get a second opinion from Dr. Pritesh on a serious diagnosis?
A: Absolutely. We encourage second opinions for cancer, neurological disease, organ failure, and any condition where the diagnosis will significantly change the pet's management. Bring previous records and we'll review them honestly.

## Vet Pharmacy
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/vet-pharmacy

Every medicine your pet needs — available on-site, the same day as diagnosis. No separate trips to a pharmacy, no delays in starting treatment.

Q: Can I buy tick prevention without a consultation?
A: Standard over-the-counter parasite control products (spot-ons, some tablets) can be purchased without a consultation. Prescription-only parasite control products (like some chewables) require a consultation first.

Q: Do you sell therapeutic diets for kidney or liver disease?
A: Yes — we stock veterinary therapeutic diets for chronic kidney disease, liver disease, skin conditions, gastrointestinal disease, and obesity management.

Q: Can you provide medicines for exotic pets like rabbits and birds?
A: Yes. We carry medications specifically dosed and formulated for exotic species, which often require different formulations than those used for dogs and cats.

Q: My dog is on long-term medication — can I just pick it up without a new consultation each time?
A: For stable long-term conditions, we can arrange repeat dispensing after an initial assessment. However, annual or biannual check-ins are recommended to ensure the medication is still appropriate and the dose is correct.

## Exotic Animal Centre
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/exotic-animal-centre

One of the very few clinics in PCMC with dedicated equipment and clinical experience for birds, rabbits, turtles, reptiles, and small exotic mammals.

Q: Is it safe to anesthetize a rabbit or bird for surgery?
A: Yes, when done correctly with gaseous anaesthesia and species-specific protocols. We use safe inhalation anaesthesia — the same approach used in specialist exotic animal hospitals. Injectable-only anaesthesia is far riskier in small exotics, and we avoid it.

Q: My rabbit hasn't eaten in 12 hours — is that serious?
A: Yes. Rabbits that stop eating for more than 6–8 hours can develop GI stasis, which becomes life-threatening within 24 hours. Call us immediately if your rabbit stops eating or producing droppings.

Q: Can you treat my turtle for shell problems?
A: Yes. We treat shell rot, soft shell (metabolic bone disease), and shell injuries. We also provide advice on correct housing, UVB lighting, and calcium supplementation to prevent recurrence.

Q: My bird is sitting fluffed up at the bottom of the cage — what should I do?
A: This is a serious warning sign. Sick birds hide illness until they can no longer compensate. A bird sitting low and fluffed is often in respiratory distress or severely ill. Call us immediately.

Q: Do you neuter rabbits in Pune?
A: Yes — rabbit neutering (castration for males, spaying for females) is one of the procedures Dr. Pritesh performs regularly using gaseous anaesthesia. Spaying is particularly important for female rabbits because over 80% of unspayed females develop uterine cancer by age 5.

## Rabbit Vet
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/rabbit-vet

Yes, we treat rabbits. Our Exotic Animal Centre sees pet rabbits for check-ups, GI stasis, dental problems, spaying and neutering, with gaseous anaesthesia, in-house blood tests and ultrasound under one roof. Exotic consultation is ₹400.

Q: Do you treat rabbits in Pune?
A: Yes. Rabbits are seen at our Exotic Animal Centre in Pimple Nilakh, Pune, for check-ups, illness, dental care and surgery. The exotic consultation is ₹400.

Q: My rabbit has stopped eating. Is it an emergency?
A: Yes. A rabbit that stops eating can develop GI stasis, which becomes life-threatening within about 24 hours. Call the clinic immediately if your rabbit stops eating or producing droppings.

Q: Do you spay and neuter rabbits?
A: Yes. Rabbit spaying and neutering are done regularly at the clinic under gaseous anaesthesia. Spaying protects female rabbits from uterine cancer, which is common in unspayed females as they age.

Q: Is anaesthesia safe for rabbits?
A: Yes, when it is done with gaseous anaesthesia, a pre-operative check and careful monitoring. That is the approach we use for rabbits; we avoid injectable-only anaesthesia in small exotics.

Q: Why are my rabbit's teeth overgrowing?
A: Because rabbit teeth grow throughout life and need constant wear from hay. Too little hay, genetics or dental disease lead to painful overgrowth, which we treat with dental rasping at the clinic.

## Bird & Parrot Vet
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/bird-vet

Yes, we treat pet birds. Budgies, cockatiels, lovebirds, conures, African greys, macaws, cockatoos, finches and canaries are seen at our Exotic Animal Centre for check-ups, illness, egg binding and surgery. Exotic consultation is ₹400.

Q: Is there an avian vet for parrots in Pune?
A: Yes. Shivraj Pet Clinic & Lab in Pimple Nilakh, Pune treats parrots and other pet birds at its Exotic Animal Centre. The exotic consultation is ₹400.

Q: Which bird species do you treat?
A: We treat budgies, cockatiels, lovebirds, conures, African greys, macaws, cockatoos, finches, canaries and many other pet birds.

Q: My bird is sitting fluffed up all day. What should I do?
A: Call the clinic the same day. A bird that stays fluffed up and inactive is usually ill and conserving heat and energy, and birds hide illness until it is advanced.

Q: Can you tell if my parrot is male or female?
A: Yes, with feather DNA sexing. We collect a few chest feathers at the clinic and send them to a specialised DNA laboratory; results usually take about 7–10 days.

Q: How often should my bird have a check-up?
A: Once a year for a healthy bird, and more often for older birds or birds with a medical condition.

## Turtle & Reptile Vet
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/turtle-reptile-vet

Yes, we treat turtles, tortoises and reptiles. Shell rot, soft or pyramided shells, swollen eyes, poor appetite and shedding problems are examined at our Exotic Animal Centre, with digital X-ray on site. Exotic consultation is ₹400.

Q: Do you treat turtles and tortoises in Pune?
A: Yes. Turtles and tortoises are seen at our Exotic Animal Centre in Pimple Nilakh, Pune, for shell problems, eye problems, poor appetite and check-ups. The exotic consultation is ₹400.

Q: What is shell rot and can it be treated?
A: Shell rot is a bacterial or fungal infection of the shell, and yes, it can be treated with cleaning, medication and correcting the habitat that caused it.

Q: Why is my turtle's shell soft?
A: A soft shell usually means metabolic bone disease from too little calcium, too little UVB light or an unbalanced diet. It is easier to prevent with correct husbandry than to reverse once set in.

Q: Do you treat iguanas and other lizards?
A: Yes. Iguanas and other common pet lizards are seen alongside turtles, tortoises, birds and small mammals at our Exotic Animal Centre.

Q: Does my tortoise need to hibernate in Pune?
A: Usually not. Most pet tortoises in Pune do not need to hibernate given the mild winters, and unsupervised hibernation carries real risk, so speak to us first.

## Guinea Pig & Hamster Vet
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/guinea-pig-hamster-vet

Yes, we treat guinea pigs, hamsters and gerbils. Overgrown teeth, vitamin C deficiency, wet tail, bladder stones and skin problems are examined and treated at our Exotic Animal Centre. Exotic consultation is ₹400.

Q: Do you treat guinea pigs and hamsters in Pune?
A: Yes. Guinea pigs, hamsters and gerbils are seen at our Exotic Animal Centre in Pimple Nilakh, Pune. The exotic consultation is ₹400.

Q: Why has my guinea pig stopped eating?
A: Usually dental disease, pain or a digestive problem, and it needs a vet visit the same day because guinea pigs should never go long without eating.

Q: Why do guinea pigs need vitamin C?
A: Because guinea pigs cannot make vitamin C themselves. Without it in the diet they develop scurvy, with weakness, joint pain and poor wound healing.

Q: What is wet tail in hamsters?
A: Wet tail is severe diarrhoea in hamsters. It can be fatal within about 48 hours without treatment, so bring your hamster in straight away.

Q: Can guinea pigs have surgery safely?
A: Yes. With proper anaesthesia and monitoring, guinea pigs can safely have surgery when it is medically necessary.

## Pathology Lab
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/pathology-lab

No referrals. No waiting days for results. Our in-house laboratory processes blood panels, urinalysis, and cytology on-site — with CBC and biochemistry results ready in 15–20 minutes, so treatment starts the same visit.

Q: How long do blood test results take?
A: CBC and biochemistry reports are generally available within 15–20 minutes in most routine cases at our in-house lab. We aim to have results ready before you leave the clinic.

Q: Does my healthy pet need blood tests?
A: Yes — annual wellness bloodwork for pets over 7 years, and before any surgery regardless of age. Many conditions (kidney disease, diabetes, liver disease) show no symptoms until advanced. Early detection changes outcomes dramatically.

Q: Do you send any tests to external labs?
A: Histopathology (tissue biopsy) and some specialized culture tests go to external labs. We'll tell you upfront which tests need to go out and what the turnaround time is.

Q: My pet needs surgery — why does it need blood tests first?
A: Pre-anaesthetic blood panels reveal hidden kidney or liver problems that affect how the body processes anaesthetic drugs. A pet that appears healthy can still have borderline organ function that requires us to adjust our protocol for safety.

Q: Can you test for tick fever?
A: Yes — we have rapid in-house tests for the most common tick-borne diseases in Pune (Ehrlichiosis, Babesiosis, Anaplasmosis). Results in 15–20 minutes.

## Digital X-Ray
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/digital-xray

High-resolution digital radiography for bones, chest, abdomen, and soft tissue. Results available immediately — no waiting, no referrals.

Q: Is X-ray safe for my pet?
A: Yes. Digital X-ray uses a very low dose of radiation. The exposure for a routine veterinary X-ray is minimal and the risk is negligible compared to the diagnostic benefit of getting an accurate diagnosis.

Q: Does my pet need to be sedated for X-ray?
A: Many pets can be X-rayed without sedation if they are calm and the area being imaged cooperates. For anxious pets, uncooperative positioning, or painful conditions where movement would be harmful, light sedation gives us clearer images and is safer for the patient.

Q: Can you do X-ray on rabbits and birds?
A: Yes — we regularly X-ray rabbits, birds, and guinea pigs. Exotic patients are handled with extra care and positioned specifically for their anatomy.

Q: How quickly will I get results?
A: Digital X-ray images are available within seconds on our monitor. Dr. Pritesh reviews and explains findings before you leave the clinic in most cases.

## Sonography
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/sonography

Non-invasive, real-time pregnancy confirmation for dogs and cats. Ultrasound detects foetal heartbeats and gives an early, safe way to confirm pregnancy well before it's visible.

Q: Is ultrasound safe for pets?
A: Completely. Ultrasound uses sound waves — no radiation. It's safe for pregnant animals, foetuses, and can be repeated as many times as needed.

Q: Does my pet need to be shaved for ultrasound?
A: A small area of fur is clipped for proper probe contact and image quality. The clip is minimal and grows back quickly.

Q: Can you tell how many puppies my dog is carrying?
A: Yes — ultrasound confirms pregnancy from about 3 weeks post-breeding. Counting is approximate on ultrasound; X-ray at 45+ days gives a more accurate litter count.

Q: My vet in another clinic said my dog has a heart murmur — what should I do?
A: We recommend consulting Dr. Pritesh who can examine your pet thoroughly and advise on the next steps, which may include referral for cardiac assessment if needed.

## Dog Neutering
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/dog-neutering

A routine procedure that reduces aggression, roaming, and the risk of testicular and prostate disease in male dogs.

Q: What age should I get my dog neutered?
A: Most vets, including ours, recommend neutering between 6 and 9 months of age, though we evaluate larger breeds case by case since some benefit from waiting until closer to a year.

Q: Will neutering change my dog's personality?
A: It typically reduces roaming, marking, and male-to-male aggression, but won't change a dog's core temperament or playfulness.

Q: How long is recovery?
A: Most dogs are back to normal activity within 10-14 days. We provide an e-collar and pain medication, and a follow-up check is included.

Q: Is anaesthesia safe for older dogs?
A: We run pre-anaesthetic bloodwork on every patient, especially seniors, using our in-house lab to assess organ function before surgery.

## Cat Spaying
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/cat-spaying

Spaying removes the ovaries and uterus, eliminating heat cycles, unwanted pregnancies, and the risk of life-threatening uterine infections.

Q: When should I spay my cat?
A: Before the first heat cycle, usually around 5-6 months, gives the strongest protection against mammary tumours later in life.

Q: My cat already had kittens — is it too late to spay?
A: No. Spaying is beneficial at any age and still removes future pregnancy and uterine disease risk.

Q: How long does recovery take?
A: Most cats are back to normal within 7-10 days. We recommend an e-collar to prevent licking the incision.

Q: Is this the same as a hysterectomy in humans?
A: Similar in concept — we remove both the uterus and ovaries, which is more thorough than ovary-only sterilization and prevents uterine disease entirely.

## Soft Tissue Surgery
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/soft-tissue-surgery

Beyond bones — surgical care for skin, organs, and internal structures, from a torn wound to an abdominal repair.

Q: My dog has a hernia — is this urgent?
A: Some hernias are stable and can be scheduled; others (especially if the bulge becomes hard, painful, or discolored) need same-day attention since tissue can become trapped. Call us and describe what you're seeing and we'll advise.

Q: Will a wound need stitches or can it heal on its own?
A: Depends on depth and location — we'll examine and tell you honestly whether it needs surgical closure or will heal fine with cleaning and bandaging.

Q: What is cherry eye and does my dog need surgery?
A: Cherry eye is a prolapsed gland in the third eyelid, common in certain breeds. It usually requires a minor surgical repositioning procedure rather than removal, to preserve normal tear production.

## Orthopedic Surgery
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/orthopedic-surgery

From a fall, an accident, or wear over time — broken bones and torn ligaments need fast, accurate diagnosis and skilled surgical repair.

Q: My dog suddenly won't put weight on a leg — what could it be?
A: Sudden limping may result from a fracture, ligament injury, spinal issue, sprain, or soft tissue trauma. Prompt veterinary examination is recommended — call us and describe what you are seeing.

Q: Can small fractures heal without surgery?
A: Some hairline fractures in small bones can be managed with strict rest and splinting. We'll tell you honestly whether your pet's specific fracture needs surgical fixation based on the X-ray.

Q: How long is recovery from orthopedic surgery?
A: Recovery depends on the condition and procedure performed. Most orthopedic patients require several weeks of restricted activity, pain management, and follow-up examinations. We provide a clear recovery plan tailored to your pet.

Q: Do you have CT scan available?
A: CT imaging is arranged through referral centres when required. We coordinate the process and ensure all records are shared so there is no delay in your pet's care.

## Dog Tumor Surgery
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/dog-tumor-surgery

Found a lump on your dog? Most skin masses are benign, but early evaluation and removal give the best outcome either way.

Q: Is every lump cancer?
A: No — most skin lumps in dogs turn out to be benign (lipomas, cysts, warts). But size, location, and growth speed all matter, which is why we examine rather than guess.

Q: Do you need to biopsy before surgery?
A: For many masses, a quick needle aspirate during the same visit gives us enough information to plan surgery. Full biopsy after removal confirms the diagnosis.

Q: How big can a mass be before it's a problem?
A: Size matters less than behaviour — a small, fast-growing, firm, or ulcerated mass is more concerning than a large, slow-growing, soft one. We'll tell you honestly which category yours falls into.

Q: Will my dog need chemotherapy after surgery?
A: Most benign and many malignant masses need only surgical removal. We'll discuss further treatment only if pathology results indicate it's necessary.

## Foreign Body Removal
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/foreign-body-removal-surgery

Toys, socks, string, bones, stones — pets swallow things that can block or tear the intestines. Fast diagnosis prevents a small problem becoming a fatal one.

Q: My dog ate a sock yesterday and seems fine — should I still bring them in?
A: Yes, get them checked. Some objects sit in the stomach for days before causing a blockage, and catching it on X-ray before symptoms worsen is far safer than waiting.

Q: My cat keeps trying to swallow string — why is this dangerous?
A: String and thread are uniquely dangerous in cats because one end can anchor (often under the tongue) while the rest is pulled into the intestines, causing a sawing injury internally. This is always an urgent case — call us right away.

Q: Will my pet need surgery every time they swallow something?
A: Not always — size, shape, and location matter. We'll image first and give you an honest assessment of whether monitoring, endoscopy, or surgery is the right call.

Q: How can I prevent this from happening again?
A: We'll talk through specific prevention strategies for your pet's habits during the visit — often it's about what's left within reach rather than a behavioural issue to "fix."

## Emergency Surgery
URL: https://www.shivrajpetclinicpune.com/services/emergency-surgery

If your pet has been hit by a vehicle, is bleeding heavily, can't breathe normally, or has a swollen, painful abdomen — call us immediately.

Q: Are you open for emergencies on Wednesday (your day off)?
A: No. Wednesday is our weekly off and we do not offer emergency service outside opening hours. On Wednesdays or after hours, please contact a 24-hour veterinary hospital.

Q: What is GDV and why is it so urgent?
A: GDV (bloat) is when the stomach fills with gas and twists on itself, cutting off blood supply. It progresses within hours and is fatal without emergency surgery — a hard, swollen abdomen with unproductive retching needs immediate attention.

Q: Should I try to treat bleeding at home first?
A: Apply firm direct pressure with a clean cloth while traveling to us, but don't delay the trip to experiment with home remedies — call us en route so we're ready when you arrive.

Q: Do you have in-house diagnostics for emergencies?
A: Yes — X-ray, ultrasound, and lab bloodwork are all on-site, so we can identify the problem within minutes of arrival rather than waiting on outside results.

## Pet care FAQs
Q: My dog has stopped eating. Should I be worried?
A: Yes. If your dog refuses food for more than 24 hours, or sooner if accompanied by vomiting, diarrhoea, lethargy, or fever, a veterinary examination is recommended.

Q: My dog is vomiting repeatedly. When should I visit the vet?
A: Repeated vomiting, especially with blood, weakness, or refusal to eat, requires prompt veterinary attention to prevent dehydration and identify the underlying cause.

Q: Why does my dog have diarrhoea?
A: Diarrhoea can result from dietary indiscretion, parasites, infections, food allergies, or more serious diseases. Persistent diarrhoea should be evaluated by a veterinarian.

Q: My dog is limping. Does it always need treatment?
A: Not always, but limping may indicate a sprain, fracture, ligament injury, arthritis, or paw injury. If it persists for more than 24 hours or is severe, veterinary examination is advised.

Q: My dog is scratching all the time. What could be the reason?
A: Common causes include fleas, ticks, mites, allergies, bacterial infections, fungal infections, and hormonal disorders.

Q: Why does my dog shake its head frequently?
A: Head shaking often indicates ear infections, ear mites, allergies, or foreign material inside the ear.

Q: My dog has a lump. Should it be removed?
A: Not every lump requires surgery, but every new lump should be examined. Early diagnosis helps determine whether it is benign or cancerous.

Q: When should I get my dog spayed or neutered?
A: The ideal age depends on breed, size, and overall health. Your veterinarian will recommend the most appropriate timing.

Q: What is pyometra in female dogs?
A: Pyometra is a serious uterine infection in unspayed females and is a surgical emergency requiring immediate treatment.

Q: My dog is having difficulty urinating. Is it an emergency?
A: Yes. Difficulty passing urine or complete inability to urinate is an emergency and requires immediate veterinary care.

Q: Does my dog need dental cleaning?
A: Dogs with tartar, bad breath, bleeding gums, or loose teeth often benefit from professional dental cleaning under anaesthesia.

Q: Why is my dog drinking excessive water?
A: Increased water intake may be associated with kidney disease, diabetes, hormonal disorders, liver disease, or certain medications.

Q: What vaccinations does my dog need?
A: Vaccination schedules vary with age and lifestyle but commonly include protection against rabies, parvovirus, distemper, hepatitis, and leptospirosis.

Q: How often should I deworm my dog?
A: Most adult dogs should be dewormed every three months, while puppies require more frequent deworming.

Q: My dog has blood in its urine. What does it mean?
A: Blood in the urine may indicate urinary tract infection, bladder stones, trauma, or other urinary diseases and requires veterinary evaluation.

Q: Can senior dogs undergo surgery safely?
A: Yes. With appropriate pre-operative testing, anaesthetic planning, and monitoring, many senior dogs safely undergo surgery.

Q: What should I do if my dog has been hit by a vehicle?
A: Keep your dog as still as possible and seek emergency veterinary care immediately, even if injuries are not immediately visible.

Q: Why is my dog coughing?
A: Coughing may be caused by kennel cough, heart disease, tracheal disorders, pneumonia, or other respiratory conditions.

Q: Do you perform emergency surgeries for dogs?
A: Yes. Emergency procedures such as Caesarean section, foreign body removal, pyometra surgery, wound repair, and bladder surgery are performed when medically indicated at our Pimple Nilakh clinic.

Q: Why choose Shivraj Pet Clinic for dog treatment?
A: We provide comprehensive medical, surgical, diagnostic, and emergency dog care in Wakad, Pimple Saudagar & PCMC, using modern equipment and evidence-based veterinary medicine.

Q: My cat has stopped eating. Is it an emergency?
A: Yes. Cats that stop eating, especially for more than 24 hours, are at risk of serious complications such as hepatic lipidosis and should be examined promptly.

Q: My cat cannot urinate. What should I do?
A: This is a life-threatening emergency, particularly in male cats. Immediate veterinary treatment is essential.

Q: Why is my cat vomiting frequently?
A: Frequent vomiting may be caused by hairballs, dietary problems, kidney disease, gastrointestinal disorders, or other medical conditions.

Q: My cat is hiding all the time. Is something wrong?
A: Cats often hide when they are in pain or unwell. Sudden behavioural changes should not be ignored.

Q: Why is my cat losing weight despite eating?
A: Weight loss may be associated with hyperthyroidism, diabetes, intestinal disease, parasites, or cancer.

Q: My cat has blood in its urine. What could be causing it?
A: Blood in the urine may result from feline lower urinary tract disease (FLUTD), urinary tract infections, bladder stones, or stress-related cystitis.

Q: Does my cat need dental treatment?
A: Cats commonly develop dental disease, which may cause pain, bad breath, drooling, and difficulty eating. Professional dental care may be required.

Q: Why is my cat breathing rapidly?
A: Rapid breathing may indicate respiratory disease, heart disease, pain, fever, or fluid around the lungs and requires immediate examination.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my cat?
A: The recommended timing depends on your cat's age and health. Your veterinarian can advise the most appropriate age.

Q: My cat has diarrhoea. Should I be concerned?
A: Persistent diarrhoea may be caused by parasites, infections, dietary intolerance, inflammatory bowel disease, or systemic illness.

Q: Why is my cat drinking more water than usual?
A: Excessive thirst may indicate kidney disease, diabetes, hyperthyroidism, or other medical conditions.

Q: My cat has a lump. Should it be checked?
A: Yes. Any new lump or swelling should be evaluated early to determine whether further treatment is needed.

Q: What vaccinations does my cat need?
A: Core vaccinations typically include protection against feline panleukopenia, herpesvirus, calicivirus, and rabies, depending on lifestyle and local recommendations.

Q: How often should my cat be dewormed?
A: Adult cats are generally dewormed every three months, while kittens require more frequent treatment.

Q: My cat is drooling excessively. Is that normal?
A: Excessive drooling may indicate dental disease, oral ulcers, poisoning, nausea, or foreign bodies in the mouth.

Q: Can older cats safely undergo surgery?
A: Yes. Many senior cats successfully undergo surgery after appropriate health assessment and anaesthetic planning.

Q: Why is my cat straining in the litter tray?
A: Straining may indicate constipation, urinary blockage, bladder disease, or other serious conditions that require prompt veterinary care.

Q: My cat is sneezing continuously. Does it need treatment?
A: Persistent sneezing may result from viral infections, allergies, nasal polyps, foreign bodies, or dental disease.

Q: Do you perform surgery for cats?
A: Yes. We perform spaying, neutering, tumour removal, bladder surgery, foreign body removal, wound repair, soft tissue surgery, and other medically indicated procedures at our Pune clinic.

Q: Why choose Shivraj Pet Clinic for cat treatment?
A: We provide dedicated feline medical and surgical care with modern diagnostics, in-house laboratory facilities, digital imaging, and personalised treatment plans for every cat in Wakad, Pimple Saudagar & Pune.

Q: Why is my bird sitting fluffed up all day?
A: A fluffed-up bird that remains inactive is often trying to conserve heat and energy. This is a common sign of illness and should be examined by an avian veterinarian as soon as possible.

Q: Why has my bird stopped eating suddenly?
A: Birds have a very fast metabolism. Even a short period without eating can become life-threatening. Loss of appetite may be caused by infections, liver disease, digestive problems, or pain.

Q: Is tail bobbing in birds normal?
A: No. Tail bobbing while breathing usually indicates respiratory distress or another serious illness and requires immediate veterinary attention.

Q: Why is my bird breathing with its beak open?
A: Open-mouth breathing may indicate respiratory disease, overheating, or severe stress. Prompt examination is recommended.

Q: My bird is bleeding. What should I do?
A: Keep your bird calm, apply gentle pressure with a clean cloth if possible, and seek veterinary care immediately. Birds can lose dangerous amounts of blood quickly.

Q: Why are my bird's droppings green?
A: Green droppings may be associated with reduced food intake, liver disease, infections, or other medical conditions. A veterinary examination is needed to determine the cause.

Q: Can birds undergo surgery safely?
A: Yes. With appropriate anaesthesia, monitoring, and surgical expertise, many birds can safely undergo necessary surgical procedures.

Q: Why is my bird vomiting seeds?
A: Seed regurgitation or vomiting may indicate crop disorders, infections, toxins, or gastrointestinal disease and should not be ignored.

Q: How often should my bird have a health check-up?
A: Healthy birds should ideally have a preventive health examination once a year, while older birds or those with medical conditions may require more frequent visits.

Q: Do you treat all pet bird species?
A: Yes. We treat budgies, cockatiels, lovebirds, African greys, macaws, cockatoos, finches, canaries, and many other pet birds at our Pune Exotic Animal Centre.

Q: Why is my turtle not eating?
A: Poor appetite can result from incorrect temperature, stress, infections, parasites, or metabolic disease. A veterinary examination can identify the underlying cause.

Q: What is shell rot?
A: Shell rot is a bacterial or fungal infection of the shell that requires cleaning, medication, and correction of habitat conditions.

Q: Why are my turtle's eyes swollen?
A: Swollen eyes are commonly caused by vitamin A deficiency, infections, or poor water quality.

Q: Why is my turtle floating sideways?
A: Uneven floating may indicate pneumonia, excessive intestinal gas, or buoyancy disorders and should be evaluated by a veterinarian.

Q: Does my turtle or tortoise need UVB lighting?
A: Yes. UVB light is essential for proper calcium metabolism, healthy bones, and shell development in both pet turtles and tortoises — glass and mesh both filter out UVB, so time behind either doesn't count.

Q: Why is my turtle's shell soft, or my tortoise's shell bumpy?
A: A soft shell in turtles or a bumpy, pyramided shell in tortoises usually points to the same root cause — inadequate calcium, insufficient UVB, or an imbalanced diet during growth. Prevention through correct husbandry matters more than treatment once it's set in.

Q: What should I feed my turtle or tortoise?
A: Diets differ by species — tortoises generally need mostly dark leafy greens with only occasional fruit, while aquatic turtles need a mix of pellets, greens, and protein. Ask us for a species-specific feeding ratio.

Q: Can turtles and tortoises undergo surgery?
A: Yes. Surgical treatment may be required for reproductive disorders, shell injuries, abscesses, and certain internal conditions.

Q: Does my tortoise need to hibernate in Pune's climate?
A: Most tortoises kept as pets in Pune don't need to hibernate given the mild winters, and unsupervised hibernation carries real risk. Talk to us before attempting it.

Q: How often should turtles and tortoises be examined?
A: Annual health check-ups help detect nutritional deficiencies, shell problems, and internal diseases before they become severe.

Q: What temperature and humidity does a pet iguana need?
A: Iguanas need a basking spot noticeably warmer than the rest of the enclosure, with humidity kept fairly high. Getting either wrong is one of the most common causes of illness we see in pet lizards.

Q: What should I feed my pet iguana?
A: Iguanas are largely herbivorous and need a varied mix of leafy greens and vegetables with appropriate calcium supplementation — not the fruit-heavy or protein-heavy diets sometimes recommended online.

Q: Why does my lizard's tail look darker or shrivelled at the tip?
A: This can indicate poor circulation, an old injury, or in some cases a retained shed. It's worth a veterinary look rather than waiting to see if it resolves on its own.

Q: My lizard is having trouble shedding its skin — is that a problem?
A: Incomplete or difficult shedding is usually a sign that humidity in the enclosure is too low. Retained shed around toes or the tail tip can restrict blood flow if it isn't resolved, so it's worth addressing promptly.

Q: Does my pet lizard need UVB lighting?
A: Yes, for the vast majority of common pet lizard species, including iguanas. Without proper UVB, they can't metabolise dietary calcium correctly, which leads to metabolic bone disease over time.

Q: Do you treat lizards and other reptiles besides turtles?
A: Yes — our Exotic Animal Centre sees iguanas and other common pet lizards alongside turtles, tortoises, birds, and small mammals.

Q: My rabbit has stopped eating. Is it an emergency?
A: Yes. Rabbits that stop eating can rapidly develop gastrointestinal stasis, which is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment.

Q: What is gastrointestinal stasis?
A: It is a condition where the digestive system slows or stops moving normally. Early treatment greatly improves the chances of recovery.

Q: Should I spay or neuter my rabbit?
A: Yes. Spaying and neutering help prevent reproductive diseases, reduce unwanted behaviours, and improve long-term health.

Q: At what age should rabbits be spayed or neutered?
A: The ideal age depends on the rabbit's breed, sex, weight, and health. Your veterinarian can recommend the best timing.

Q: Why are my rabbit's teeth overgrowing?
A: Rabbit teeth grow continuously. Poor diet, genetics, or dental disease can prevent normal wear and lead to painful overgrowth.

Q: Can rabbits safely undergo anaesthesia?
A: Yes. With proper pre-operative assessment and monitoring, rabbits can safely undergo many surgical procedures.

Q: Why is my rabbit passing very small droppings?
A: Small droppings often indicate reduced gut movement or inadequate food intake and should be evaluated promptly.

Q: Can rabbits develop uterine cancer?
A: Yes. Unspayed female rabbits have a high risk of uterine cancer as they age, making spaying an important preventive procedure.

Q: What should rabbits eat daily?
A: Unlimited grass hay, fresh water, leafy vegetables, and a measured amount of quality pellets form the basis of a healthy rabbit diet.

Q: Do you perform rabbit surgeries?
A: Yes. We perform rabbit spays, neuters, tumour removal, wound repair, dental procedures, and other surgical treatments at our Pimple Nilakh clinic.

Q: Why has my guinea pig stopped eating?
A: Guinea pigs should never go long without eating. Loss of appetite may indicate dental disease, pain, digestive problems, or other serious illnesses.

Q: Why do guinea pigs need vitamin C?
A: Unlike humans, guinea pigs cannot produce vitamin C. A deficiency can cause weakness, joint pain, poor wound healing, and other health problems.

Q: Can guinea pigs develop bladder stones?
A: Yes. Bladder stones are relatively common and may cause pain, blood in the urine, or difficulty urinating.

Q: Why is my guinea pig losing weight?
A: Weight loss may result from dental disease, chronic illness, infections, parasites, or inadequate nutrition.

Q: Can guinea pigs undergo surgery safely?
A: Yes. With proper anaesthesia and monitoring, many guinea pigs safely undergo surgery when medically necessary.

Q: What is bumblefoot?
A: Bumblefoot is a painful infection of the feet caused by pressure sores, obesity, poor hygiene, or unsuitable cage flooring.

Q: Why are my guinea pig's teeth becoming too long?
A: Abnormal tooth wear or dental disease can lead to overgrown teeth that interfere with eating.

Q: How often should guinea pigs have veterinary check-ups?
A: Annual examinations are recommended, with more frequent visits for senior pets or those with chronic illnesses.

Q: What foods should guinea pigs eat every day?
A: Good-quality hay, fresh vegetables rich in vitamin C, fresh water, and guinea pig-specific pellets are essential for good health.

Q: Do you provide emergency treatment for guinea pigs?
A: Yes. Guinea pigs showing loss of appetite, breathing difficulty, severe weakness, urinary problems, or injuries should be examined immediately at our Pimple Nilakh clinic.
